rv.q: The final scene, where Beatrice and Benedick finally come together, is absolutely joyful.
This light-hearted take on Shakespeare’s story of matched wits and combative gender dynamics tells the familiar tale with maximum levity.
In Pippa Nixon’s Beatrice and Ken Nwosu’s Benedick, it gives us one of the most charming accounts of Shakespeare’s sparring partners this decade.

The “skirmish of wit” between the tart-tongued proto-feminist Beatrice, embodied with mischievous vivacity by Pippa Nixon, and Ken Nwosu’s wry, equally marriage-wary Benedick is a pleasure to hear and see.
In its charms it is winning: insuppressibly crowd-pleasing, eminently worth seeing.
It’s the more serious bits where it struggles.
Chelsea Walker’s Much Ado is a triumphant joy.
This is Shakespeare exactly as it should be experienced: lively, funny, dramatic, and completely engaging, brought to life by an exceptionally talented cast.

All is put right in time for the sort of collectively joyful curtain call that defines the Globe at its very best, of which this Much Ado – opening just in time for the summer solstice – is a shining example.
Walker’s command of the tonal shift is assured: we are laughing one minute and stunned into silence by the brutality of the accusations the next.
It is a delight on a summer's evening: a delicately calibrated and confident treat.
This version is hugely enjoyable, even if some of the darker intent doesn’t quite pack the punch that it could.

When the Messenger observes that Beatrice is clearly annoyed with Benedick, “The gentleman is not in your books,” her stinging response, “An he were, I would burn my study” gets a huge laugh as opposed to the more customary ripple of amusement.
Walker’s direction is a masterclass in smooth storytelling.

This version of Shakespeare’s classic deception comedy manages to be both minimalist and maximalist at once, starting with an ensemble of costumes ranging from TikTok-favoured butter yellow sundresses to BDSM harnesses, by way of sharp 1970s tailoring, offering a confused sense of time and place.
This is a sublime production of About Nothing that captures the hearts and minds of its audience.

So there are few verse speeches during which an actor who might be competing against the elements will be buoyed by the metre. There were no extraneous noises in gorgeous weather on press night at the outdoor Globe Theatre save for a military-sounding plane that flashed over the venue and blended with the martial backdrop.
Chelsea Walker’s About Nothing succeeds because it trusts Shakespeare’s text while illuminating its enduring relevance, producing a comedy that feels both timeless and thoroughly contemporary.

cn.t: Walker's fizzy, summery Globe production delights with Nixon and Nwosu's sparkling chemistry as Beatrice and Benedick, though some find it tonally uneven. The playful staging honors the comedy's light and shade with maximum levity.
